entities.name: Temple of Apollo Zoster
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Apollo Zoster ('Girt', Apollo of the Girdle) at Vouliagmeni on the Attic coast of ancient Greece — one of the few surviving attested Apollo sanctuaries in Attica outside Athens itself — was an ancient Greek religious site associated with the myth that Leto (mother of Apollo and Artemis) loosened her girdle here during or after her labor, giving rise to the epithet 'Zoster' (girdle-wearer). The sanctuary served the deme of Halai Aixonides in southern Attica.

The mythological narrative centered on Leto: fleeing Hera's wrath after her conception by Zeus, Leto traveled to find a safe place to give birth. At the Zoster Cape on the Attic coast, she loosened or removed her girdle in preparation for or relief after labor — giving the site its distinctive Apollo epithet. The sanctuary thus marked a perceived moment in the divine birth narrative that was central to Apollo's origin myth.

Archaeologically, the Zoster sanctuary is known primarily from literary and epigraphic sources rather than from substantial excavated remains. Its location at Vouliagmeni (modern southern suburb of Athens, now famous for its natural salt lake and luxury resort area) has been confirmed by ancient sources including Strabo. The sanctuary served the local deme population's religious needs and participated in the broader network of Attic Apollo worship that centered on Delos and Delphi as its most sacred nodes. The Temple of Apollo Zoster represents the dense network of local sacred sites that structured ancient Greek religious geography.
